kalp-varah: Beginning of the Shveta Varaha Kalpa
In the Puranas one kalpa is a single day of Lord Brahma — 4.32 billion years. The present kalpa is named after Lord Varaha, and we live in its seventh manvantara.
varah-avatar-vishnu: Hiranyaksha dragged the Earth down to Rasatala. Lord Vishnu took the form of a boar, slew him, and lifted Bhudevi back into place on his tusks.
manu: Born of Lord Brahma, the first Manu and his wife Shatarupa began the human race. Uttanapada and Priyavrata were their sons.
dhruv-tara: Hurt by his stepmother's insult, the boy Dhruva did fierce penance in Madhuvan. Pleased, Narayana gave him an unmoving place in the sky — today's Pole Star.
sati-daksh-shiv-shaktipeeth: When Daksha insulted Mahadev at his yajna, Sati gave up her body in yogic fire. Virabhadra destroyed the yajna; wherever Sati's body fell, a Shakti Peeth arose.
prithu: When the Earth hid her grain, King Prithu milked her in the form of a cow to bring back food and herbs. The Earth is called "Prithvi" after him.
samudra-manthan-kurma: Samudra Manthan and the Kurma Avatar
Devas and asuras churned the Ocean of Milk with Mount Mandara as the rod and Vasuki as the rope. Lord Kurma held the mountain on his back, and fourteen treasures came out.
neelkanth-shiv: The Halahala poison from the churning began to burn all creation. Mahadev drank it and held it in his throat, and was called Neelkanth, the blue-throated one.
mohini-kumbh: Mohini Avatar and the Story of Kumbh
As Mohini, Vishnu served the amrit to the devas. The four places where drops from the amrit pot fell are where the Kumbh Mela is held today.
manvantar: The age of the seventh Manu, Vaivasvata Manu, began. This is the present manvantara.
matsya-avatar: Matsya Avatar and the Great Flood
In the waters of the pralaya, Lord Matsya tied Manu's boat to his horn and saved it, protecting the Vedas and the Saptarishis.
ikshvaku-suryavansh: Vaivasvata Manu founded Ayodhya, and the Suryavansh (Solar Dynasty) began with his son Ikshvaku. Harishchandra, Bhagiratha and Shri Ram were later born in this line.
pururava-chandravansh: The Chandravansh began with Pururava, son of Budha and Ila. Yadu, Kuru, the Pandavas and Shri Krishna were born in this line.
satyug: The first yuga of the present, 28th mahayuga. Dharma stood on all four legs — truth, austerity, compassion and charity.
narsingh-prahlad-holi: Hiranyakashipu tried to kill his devotee son Prahlada. The Lord burst out of a pillar as Narasimha and slew him on the threshold at dusk.
harishchandra: To keep his word, Harishchandra gave up his kingdom, wife and son and became a servant at the cremation ground. Unshaken in truth, he became immortal.
treta-yug: Dharma now stood on three legs. This is the age of the Vamana, Parashurama and Shri Ram avatars.
vaman-bali-onam: Vamana asked the generous King Bali for three steps of land and measured all the worlds in two. Bali offered his head for the third step and became king of Patala.
bhagirath-ganga: To free his ancestors, Bhagiratha did hard penance. Mahadev caught Ganga's force in his matted hair, and Mother Ganga came down to Earth.
vishwamitra-gayatri: Defeated by Vasishtha, King Kaushika did penance for thousands of years. In the end Vasishtha himself called him Brahmarshi — he is the seer of the Gayatri Mantra.
parshuram: Parashurama, son of Jamadagni, destroyed the tyrant kings. Tradition says he raised the land of Konkan and Kerala from the sea.
agastya: Sage Agastya asked the ever-rising Vindhya mountain to bow and went south. He is honoured as the first teacher of South India's rishi tradition.
ram-janm-ramnavami: On Chaitra Shukla Navami, Lord Vishnu was born as Shri Ram to King Dasharatha and Mother Kaushalya. Ram Navami is celebrated on this day.
sita-swayamvar-vivah-panchami: King Janaka's condition was to string Shiva's bow. When Shri Ram lifted it, the bow broke, and Mother Sita placed the wedding garland on him.
vanvas-chitrakoot: Kaikeyi's two boons sent Ram into exile for fourteen years. Sita and Lakshmana went with him; Bharata ruled with Ram's sandals on the throne.
sita-haran-jatayu: Using the trick of the golden deer to draw Ram and Lakshmana away, Ravana carried off Sita. Jatayu tried to stop him and died a hero's death.
hanuman-lanka: Hanuman leapt across the ocean, gave Ram's ring to Mother Sita in the Ashoka Vatika, and set Lanka on fire.
ram-setu-rameshwaram: Led by Nala and Nila, the vanara army built a bridge over the sea with stones marked with Ram's name. At Rameswaram, Shri Ram installed a Shivalinga.
ravan-dussehra: After a fierce war, Shri Ram killed Ravana. This victory of dharma over adharma is celebrated on Dussehra.
diwali-ram-rajya: Shri Ram's Return and Ram Rajya
When Shri Ram returned to Ayodhya after the exile, the people lit lamps — the tradition of Deepavali. His reign is remembered as the ideal Ram Rajya.
valmiki-ramayan: Grief at a krauncha bird's death brought the first shloka from the lips of Adikavi Valmiki. He went on to compose the Ramayana of 24,000 shlokas.
dwapar-yug: Dharma now stood on two legs. This is the age of Shri Krishna and the Mahabharata.
bharat-shakuntala: Emperor Bharata was the son of Dushyanta and Shakuntala. By tradition the land is called "Bharatvarsha" after him.
kuru-kurukshetra: King Kuru tilled this land with penance and dharma, so it is called Dharmakshetra Kurukshetra. The Kuru dynasty began with him.
vyas-guru-purnima: Krishna Dvaipayana, son of Sage Parashara and Satyavati, was born on an island in the Yamuna. He later divided the Vedas and composed the Mahabharata.
bhishma-pratigya: For his father Shantanu's happiness, Devavrata vowed lifelong celibacy and gave up the throne — from then on he was called "Bhishma".
krishna-janm-janmashtami: At midnight on Bhadrapada Krishna Ashtami, Shri Krishna appeared to Devaki and Vasudeva in Kamsa's prison. Vasudeva carried him across the Yamuna to Gokul.
vrindavan-leela-govardhan: Stealing butter, taming Kaliya, lifting Govardhan and the Maha Raas — the leelas of Braj made Kanha the darling of every heart.
kans-vadh: At the bow festival in Mathura, the young Krishna killed Kamsa and freed his parents and Ugrasena from prison.
sandipani-sudama: In Ujjain, Krishna and Balarama learned the 64 arts from Guru Sandipani in 64 days; here Krishna became friends with Sudama.
dwarka: To protect his people from Jarasandha's repeated attacks, Shri Krishna built the golden city of Dwarka on the seashore.
draupadi-arjun: Disguised as a brahmin, Arjuna pierced the eye of the spinning fish and won Draupadi.
indraprastha-rajsuya: The Pandavas turned Khandavaprastha into Indraprastha. At Yudhishthira's Rajasuya yajna, Shri Krishna received the first worship.
chirharan-draupadi: The Dice Game and Draupadi's Honour
Through Shakuni's deceit the Pandavas lost everything. In the full assembly, Shri Krishna saved Draupadi's honour with an endless sari.
pashupatastra-kirat: During the exile, Arjuna did penance to Mahadev. Shiva tested him in the guise of a hunter (Kirata), then, pleased, gave him the Pashupatastra.
shanti-doot: Shri Krishna as the Messenger of Peace
To avert war, Shri Krishna asked for just five villages for the Pandavas. Duryodhana refused to give even land the size of a needle's point.
gita-updesh-geeta-jayanti: The Teaching of the Bhagavad Gita
To Arjuna, lost in doubt, Shri Krishna taught karma, jnana and bhakti and showed his Vishvarupa. Gita Jayanti falls on Margashirsha Shukla Ekadashi.
mahabharat-yudh: Eighteen days, eighteen akshauhini armies. The Kauravas fell and dharma was restored.
bhishma-sahasranam: Bhishma on the Bed of Arrows
Blessed to choose his time of death, Bhishma waited on a bed of arrows for Uttarayana and taught Yudhishthira dharma and the Vishnu Sahasranama.
yudhishthir: After the war Yudhishthira became king and performed the Ashvamedha yajna.
yadav: Cursed by sages, the Yadavas fought among themselves at Prabhas and perished.
bhalka-tirth: Shri Krishna Returns to His Abode
After a hunter's arrow struck his foot, Shri Krishna ended his earthly leela. The spot is known today as Bhalka Tirth.
kalyug: Kali Yuga began as Shri Krishna departed. Dharma now stands on one leg, but in this age chanting the Lord's name is held to be the greatest path.
pandav-swarg: Handing the kingdom to Parikshit, the Pandavas walked toward the Himalaya. Only Yudhishthira reached heaven in his body.
ved-vyas: Vyasa divided the Veda into four — Rig, Yajur, Sama and Atharva — and gave each to a disciple.
bhagwat-katha-shukdev: Shukadeva Recites the Bhagavata to Parikshit
Knowing he would die in seven days, King Parikshit heard the Shrimad Bhagavatam from Shukadeva on the bank of the Ganga — the origin of the Bhagavata Saptah tradition.
janmejay: To avenge his father Parikshit, Janamejaya held a snake sacrifice; Sage Astika had it stopped. The Mahabharata was first recited at this sacrifice.
naimisharanya-sut: At Naimisharanya, Suta told the Puranas to Shaunaka and the other rishis — most Puranas open with this very dialogue.
shore-temple: Built by the sea in the time of the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II, this stone temple is dedicated to both Shiva and Vishnu.
kailasanathar-kanchi: The oldest stone Shiva temple of Kanchi, built in the time of the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha).
andal: The only woman among the twelve Alvar saints, Andal composed the Tiruppavai and took Lord Ranganatha as her husband.
kailasa-ellora: In the time of the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I, the whole Kailasa temple was carved top-down out of a single rock.
adi-shankaracharya: Adi Shankaracharya — Advaita and the Four Maths
Born in Kaladi, Kerala, Shankaracharya spread Advaita Vedanta and founded maths in the four directions of the land.
kedarnath: The highest of the twelve Jyotirlingas. Tradition says the Pandavas sought Shiva here and Shankaracharya restored the temple.
badrinath: The abode of Lord Badrinarayan on the Alaknanda. Tradition says Shankaracharya took the murti out of Narada Kund and installed it.
tirupati-balaji: Lord Venkateswara on the seven hills. The oldest inscriptions here date to around the ninth century.
chidambaram-nataraja: The abode of Shiva's Ananda Tandava. Chola kings covered its roof in gold; here Shiva is worshipped as the element of space (akasha).
brihadeeswara: The Chola emperor Rajaraja I built this huge Shiva temple in 1010 CE. Its tower is among the tallest in South India.
ramanujacharya: Ramanujacharya taught Vishishtadvaita and opened the door of bhakti to all. Srirangam was his main centre.
modhera: A Sun temple built in 1026 CE under the Chalukya king Bhimadeva I, with a beautiful stepped tank, the Surya Kund, in front.
kandariya-mahadeva: Built under the Chandela kings, this Shiva temple is a fine example of the Nagara style, its tower rising like Mount Kailash.
lingaraj: A grand eleventh-century temple in the Kalinga style, where Harihara — Shiva and Vishnu in one form — is worshipped.
basavanna: Basavanna — Vachanas and the Anubhava Mantapa
The twelfth-century Shiva devotee Basavanna opposed caste through his Kannada vachanas and seated everyone as equals in the Anubhava Mantapa.
jagannath-puri: The present temple, built under the Ganga king Anantavarman Chodaganga, is one of the Char Dham. Its Rath Yatra is world-famous.
rameswaram: A Jyotirlinga linked to the Shivalinga installed by Shri Ram. Its long corridors were built after the twelfth century.
jayadeva: The poet Jayadeva wrote the Gita Govinda in Sanskrit; its songs are still sung in the Jagannath temple at Puri.
pandharpur: Vithoba stands on a brick for his devotee Pundalik. Inscriptions go back to the 12th–13th centuries; lakhs of Warkaris come on Ashadhi Ekadashi.
madhvacharya: Madhvacharya taught Dvaita philosophy and installed the murti of Bala Krishna at Udupi, still worshipped today.
konark: The Ganga king Narasimhadeva I built this temple as the chariot of the Sun god, with twelve pairs of stone wheels.
namdev: The Warkari saint Namdev of Maharashtra sang abhangs of devotion to Vitthal. His verses are also in the Guru Granth Sahib.
dnyaneshwar: At sixteen, Sant Dnyaneshwar wrote the Dnyaneshwari, a Marathi commentary on the Gita, and took samadhi at Alandi.
ramananda: Ramananda opened Ram bhakti to all. Kabir, Ravidas and many saints are linked to his tradition.
vaishno-devi: In the holy cave on Trikuta mountain, the Mother is present as three pindis — Mahakali, Mahalakshmi and Mahasaraswati.
lal-ded: The Shiva yogini Lal Ded of Kashmir composed vakhs in Kashmiri that are still spoken in homes there.
srirangam: Hidden during the invasions, the murti of Ranganatha came back to Srirangam around 1371 CE. It is among the largest functioning temple complexes in the world.
srisailam: Both a Jyotirlinga and a Shakti Peeth (Bhramaramba). The temple was greatly expanded in the Vijayanagara period.
annamacharya: A devotee of Venkateswara of Tirumala, Annamacharya composed about 32,000 sankirtanas — the grandfather of Telugu song-poetry.
narsinh-mehta: The first great poet of Gujarati, Narsinh Mehta wrote songs of Krishna bhakti. Gandhiji's favourite bhajan, Vaishnav Jan To, is his.
kabir: The weaver-saint Kabir of Kashi struck at hypocrisy with his dohas and taught devotion to the formless Ram.
sankardev: Assam's saint Sankardev joined all of Assam in Krishna bhakti through Ekasarana Naam Dharma, the Namghar, Borgeet and Ankia Naat.
ravidas: Sant Ravidas of Kashi said: if the mind is pure, the Ganga is in your water bowl. Meerabai regarded him as her guru.
surdas: In the Sursagar, Surdas of the Ashtachhap sang child Krishna's leelas as if he had seen them with his own eyes.
vallabhacharya: Vallabhacharya taught Shuddhadvaita and the Pushtimarg, where the Lord's grace is everything. Shrinathji is worshipped in this tradition.
purandara-dasa: The grandfather of Carnatic music, Purandara Dasa composed thousands of Kannada songs and set the order in which music is learned.
chaitanya-mahaprabhu: Born in Navadvipa, Chaitanya Mahaprabhu carried the sankirtan of the Hare Krishna Mahamantra to every home.
meera-bai: The Rajput queen Meerabai took Giridhar Gopal as her all, left the palace and sang songs of bhakti.
dwarkadhish: One of the Char Dham. Tradition says Krishna's great-grandson Vajranabha built the first temple; the present one is from later centuries.
kanakadasa: Moved by the devotion of Kanakadasa of the Kuruba community, the Krishna murti at Udupi turned toward him — that window is called Kanakana Kindi.
virupaksha-hampi: The main Shiva temple of the Vijayanagara capital. King Krishnadevaraya built its tall gopuram in 1510 CE.
eknath: Sant Eknath of Paithan wrote a Marathi commentary on the Bhagavata, prepared a pure text of the Dnyaneshwari, and awakened society with his bharuds.
kamakhya: The Kamakhya temple, foremost among the Shakti Peeths, was rebuilt in 1565 CE by the Koch king Naranarayan.
tulsidas: On Ram Navami of Samvat 1631, Goswami Tulsidas began writing the Ramcharitmanas in Ayodhya.
guruvayur: Kerala's most famous Krishna temple. In 1586, Melpathur Narayana Bhattathiri composed the Narayaneeyam here.
baidyanath: A Jyotirlinga whose story is linked to Ravana. In Sawan, Kanwariyas carry Ganga water here from Sultanganj.
meenakshi: The temple of Mother Meenakshi and Sundareswarar (Shiva). Its vast present form was mostly built under the Nayak kings in the 16th–17th centuries.
tukaram: The abhangs of Sant Tukaram of Dehu are still sung by Warkaris on the pilgrimage to Pandharpur.
samarth-ramdas: The Hanuman devotee Samarth Ramdas wrote the Manache Shlok and Dasbodh and built Hanuman temples in many places.
padmanabhaswamy: Lord Padmanabha reclining on Sheshanaga. In the 1730s King Marthanda Varma renovated the temple and dedicated his kingdom to the Lord.
mahakaleshwar: Mahakal, the south-facing Jyotirlinga. The present temple was rebuilt in the eighteenth century by the Maratha chief Ranoji Shinde.
trimbakeshwar: At the source of the Godavari, a Jyotirlinga with three faces — Brahma, Vishnu and Mahesh. Peshwa Nanasaheb began building the present temple.
tyagaraja: A devotee of Shri Ram, Tyagaraja composed thousands of kritis. His Pancharatna kritis are a treasure of Carnatic music.
grishneshwar: The twelfth Jyotirlinga, with the story of the devotee Ghushma. Queen Ahilyabai Holkar rebuilt it in the eighteenth century.
muthuswami-dikshitar: One of the Trinity of Carnatic music, Dikshitar composed Sanskrit kritis on gods, goddesses and temples.
kashi-vishwanath: Foremost among the twelve Jyotirlingas. The present temple was built in 1780 CE by Queen Ahilyabai Holkar.
swaminarayan: Born in Chhapaiya, Ghanshyam left home as a boy and founded the Swaminarayan Sampradaya in Gujarat.
bhimashankar: A Jyotirlinga at the source of the Bhima river, where Shiva slew the asura Bhima. Nana Phadnavis built its hall in the eighteenth century.
siddhivinayak: Laxman Vithu and Deubai Patil built a small temple in 1801; today it is among India's most famous Ganesh temples.
kalighat: A temple of Mother Kali in the Shakti Peeth tradition. The present temple was built in 1809 CE; the name of Kolkata is linked to it.
gangotri: The temple of Mother Ganga on the Bhagirathi, where the Bhagirath Shila lies. The Gorkha general Amar Singh Thapa built it in the early nineteenth century.
ramakrishna: Ramakrishna Paramahamsa, worshipper of Mother Kali, said: as many faiths, so many paths. Swami Vivekananda was his disciple.
sarada-devi: Wife and disciple of Ramakrishna Paramahamsa, Sarada Devi came to be called the Sangha Janani — the mother of all.
banke-bihari: The present temple of Thakur Banke Bihari, who appeared to Swami Haridas, was built in 1864 CE.
dayananda-saraswati: Swami Dayananda and the Arya Samaj
Swami Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in Mumbai in 1875 and gave the call: back to the Vedas.
gajanan-maharaj: On 23 February 1878 an avadhuta was seen in Shegaon eating food from a discarded leaf plate — he came to be known as Gajanan Maharaj.
vivekananda: At the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions, Swami Vivekananda's "Sisters and Brothers of America" carried India's message to the world.
ramana-maharshi: Sixteen-year-old Venkataraman awoke to the Self through an experience of death; in 1896 he came to Arunachala and stayed there all his life.
anandamayi-ma: Born in Bengal, Anandamayi Ma entered states of samadhi from childhood. Her ashrams grew up across the country.
sri-aurobindo: The revolutionary Aurobindo Ghose came to Puducherry in 1910, turned fully to yoga and gave the path of Integral Yoga.
shirdi-sai: Sai Baba of Shirdi taught shraddha and saburi — faith and patience. He took samadhi on Vijayadashami in 1918.
paramahansa-yogananda: In 1920 Yogananda went to America and carried Kriya Yoga to the West. His Autobiography of a Yogi is read across the world.
swami-sivananda: A doctor turned sannyasi, Swami Sivananda founded the Divine Life Society in Rishikesh in 1936 — serve, love, give, meditate.
sabarimala: The temple of Lord Ayyappa in the forests of the Western Ghats. Rebuilt after the 1950 fire; devotees come after a 41-day vow.
somnath: Somnath, the first Jyotirlinga, was broken and rebuilt many times. A new temple was built after Independence and consecrated in 1951.
neem-karoli-baba: Neem Karoli Baba and Kainchi Dham
The Hanuman devotee Neem Karoli Baba founded Kainchi Dham on 15 June 1964; a bhandara is held on this day every year.
prabhupada-iskcon: Arriving in America at the age of seventy, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada founded ISKCON in 1966.
akshardham-delhi: This vast stone temple dedicated to Bhagwan Swaminarayan opened in 2005.
prem-mandir: A white marble temple of Radha-Krishna and Sita-Ram built by Jagadguru Kripalu Maharaj, opened in 2012.
ram-mandir-ayodhya: Pran Pratishtha of Shri Ram Lalla, Ayodhya
On 22 January 2024, Shri Ram Lalla was consecrated in the new Ram Mandir at Ayodhya.
aaj-today: About 5,128 years of Kali Yuga have passed. On this journey through time, today is here.
nashik-kumbh-2027: In 2027 the Simhastha Kumbh's Amrit Snan will be held on the Godavari at Nashik and Trimbakeshwar.
ujjain-simhastha-2028: In 2028 the Simhastha Kumbh will be held on the Kshipra at Ujjain, the city of Mahakal.
sankirtan: The Age of Naam Sankirtan in Kali Yuga
Tradition says the Lord's naam sankirtan will flourish for about the first 10,000 years of Kali Yuga.
dharm: The Bhagavatam says that in Kali Yuga truth, compassion and austerity will keep declining and dharma will stand on one leg alone.
kalyug-bhavishya: A prophecy of the Puranas — instead of protecting the people, rulers will start seizing their wealth.
aayu: Toward the end of Kali Yuga, human lifespan, strength and memory will keep shrinking.
ved: According to the Puranas, Vedic knowledge and the tradition of yajna will slowly begin to vanish.
prakriti: Rivers, Herbs and Rain Will Fail
The Earth's fertility will fall and rain will become irregular — a picture of the last days of Kali Yuga.
kalki-avatar: At the end of Kali Yuga, Lord Vishnu will be born as Kalki in the village of Shambhala, in the home of Vishnuyasha.
kalki-parshuram: According to the Kalki Purana, the immortal Parashurama will teach Kalki the art of weapons on Mahendra mountain.
kalki-devdatt: Riding the white horse Devadatta, sword in hand, Lord Kalki will end adharma.
maru-devapi: Kept alive by yogic power, Maru (Solar dynasty) and Devapi (Lunar dynasty) will return from Kalapa village and restart both royal lines.
kalyug-ant: The Kali Yuga of 432,000 years will be complete.
satyug-wapsi: Satya Yuga will come again, and the wheel of time will turn anew.
har-ki-pauri: By tradition King Vikramaditya built this ghat on the Ganga in memory of his brother Bhartrihari. The Brahmakund is here.
elephanta-caves: Rock-cut caves on an island near Mumbai, with the huge three-faced Sadashiva image of Shiva.
badami-cave-temples: Cave 3 at Badami, with an inscription of the Chalukya king Mangalesha, carries Vishnu as Trivikrama, Narasimha and on Shesha.
martand-sun-temple: King Lalitaditya Muktapida of Kashmir built a grand temple of the Sun god on a high plateau; its ruins still stand.
abhinavagupta: The great Kashmiri teacher Abhinavagupta wrote the Tantraloka and raised Shaiva philosophy, aesthetics and the Natyashastra commentary to new heights.
omkareshwar: Omkareshwar, one of the twelve Jyotirlingas, stands on an Om-shaped island in the middle of the Narmada.
gorakhnath: Guru Gorakhnath and the Nath tradition
Gorakhnath, disciple of Matsyendranath, spread Hatha Yoga and the Nath tradition across India.
amarnath: The pilgrimage to the ice lingam that forms in a Himalayan cave. Kalhana Rajatarangini mentions the Amareshvara tirtha.
nimbarka: Nimbarkacharya taught Dvaitadvaita and placed the joint worship of Radha and Krishna at the centre.
vedanta-desika: Vedanta Desika, a great teacher of the Ramanuja tradition, wrote over a hundred works and strengthened Shri Vaishnava thought.
udupi-krishna: Madhvacharya installed at Udupi the image of child Krishna found hidden in a lump of clay brought by the sea.
chokhamela: Chokhamela, born in the Mahar community, was a devotee of Vitthal whose abhangas are still sung. His samadhi is at the temple steps.
vidyaranya: Inspired by Vidyaranya of Sringeri, Harihara and Bukka founded the Vijayanagara empire.
hit-harivansh: Hit Harivansh and the Radhavallabh tradition
Hit Harivansh Mahaprabhu founded the Radhavallabh tradition with Shri Radha at its centre.
swami-haridas: Swami Haridas, guru of the great singer Tansen, manifested the image of Banke Bihari in Nidhivan.
dadu-dayal: Dadu Dayal, a saint of nirguna bhakti, spoke in simple words of love and of Ram living in every heart.
raskhan: Born into a Muslim family, Raskhan was so absorbed in love for Krishna that his savaiyas are still sung in Braj.
govind-dev-temple: Raja Man Singh of Amer built the seven-storey red-stone Govind Dev temple, one of the grandest in North India.
nathdwara-shrinathji: The chariot carrying Shrinathji from Govardhan stopped in Mewar, and Nathdwara grew around it.
bhadrachalam: Bhakta Ramadasu (Kancharla Gopanna) built the Sita-Rama temple on the Godavari and kept singing to Ram even in prison.
khatu-shyam: Barbarika, the hero of the Mahabharata who gave his head to Shri Krishna, is worshipped at Khatu as Shyam.
ramprasad-sen: Ramprasad Sen, poet-devotee of Mother Kali, gave Bengal Shyama Sangeet — songs that speak to the Mother like a child.
salasar-balaji: An image of Hanuman found while ploughing at Asota village came to Salasar by the resolve of the devotee Mohandas.
dakshineswar-kali-temple: Rani Rashmoni built the temple of Mother Bhavatarini Kali on the Ganga, where Ramakrishna Paramahamsa became the priest.
lahiri-mahasaya: After his initiation into Kriya Yoga by Mahavatar Babaji in the Himalaya, Lahiri Mahasaya taught it while living as a householder.
belur-math: Swami Vivekananda founded Belur Math on the Ganga as the headquarters of the Ramakrishna Math and Mission.
shiv-parvati-vivah: Sati was reborn as Parvati, daughter of Himavan, and through fierce tapas won Mahadev as her husband.
ganesh-janm-pratham-pujya: Parvati shaped a son from turmeric paste; Shiva revived him with an elephant head and made him the first to be worshipped.
kartikeya-tarakasur: Tarakasura could die only by a son of Shiva; Kartikeya, born of Shiva's radiance, slew him and became commander of the gods.
durga-mahishasura-mardini: Born from the combined radiance of the gods, Mother Durga fought for nine days and slew Mahishasura.
markandeya-mahamrityunjay: Destined to die at sixteen, Markandeya embraced the Shiva-linga; Mahadev stopped Yama and made him immortal.
gajendra-moksha: Caught by a crocodile, the elephant king called on the Lord; Shri Hari rushed on Garuda and freed him with the chakra.
narad-muni-devarshi: With his vina and the name of Narayana, Devarshi Narada roamed the three worlds and set Dhruva, Prahlada and Valmiki on the path of devotion.
savitri-satyavan: Following Yama who had taken her husband's life, Savitri won Satyavan back through wisdom and devotion.
nachiketa-yama: Young Nachiketa refused wealth and kingdoms and asked Yama the truth beyond death; this is the Katha Upanishad.
atri-anasuya-dattatreya: Atri, Anasuya and the Birth of Dattatreya
The Trimurti, come to test Anasuya, became her sons; Dattatreya, born of Vishnu, is worshipped in three-faced form.
hanuman-janm: Son of Kesari and Anjana, born by the blessing of Vayu, the child Hanuman leapt to swallow the sun thinking it a fruit.
ahalya-uddhar: Ahalya, frozen in penance under a curse, was freed the moment Shri Ram arrived.
kevat-prasang: Before ferrying the Lord across the Ganga, Kevat washed his feet; asked for payment, he said, carry me across the ocean of life.
bharat-milap-paduka: Bharat came to bring Rama back, returned with his sandals on his head, and ruled for fourteen years from Nandigram as a servant.
jatayu-balidan: The aged vulture-king Jatayu fought Ravana as he carried off Sita; Rama performed his last rites as a son would.
shabari-ber: Shri Ram lovingly ate the berries Shabari had tasted for him after waiting for years on her guru's word.
ram-hanuman-milan-sugriv: Rama Meets Hanuman; Friendship with Sugriva
Hanuman, disguised as a brahmin, recognised the Lord; with fire as witness, Rama and Sugriva became friends.
lakshman-shakti-sanjivani: When Lakshmana fell to Meghnad's weapon, Hanuman carried back a whole mountain and the Sanjivani herb saved him.
lav-kush: Born at Valmiki's ashram, Sita's sons Lava and Kusha sang the Ramayana before their father Shri Ram at his ashvamedha.
kaliya-daman: Dancing on the hoods of the serpent Kaliya, who had poisoned the Yamuna, young Krishna forced him to leave the river.
govardhan-leela: To shield Braj from Indra's storm, Krishna held up Govardhan hill on one finger for seven days.
rukmini-haran: Betrothed against her will to Shishupala, Rukmini wrote to Krishna, who carried her away from the temple in his chariot.
sudama-milan: Poor Sudama reached Dwarka with a handful of rice; without being asked, Krishna filled his home with wealth.
eklavya-guru-dakshina: Ekalavya learnt archery before a clay image of Drona and gave his thumb as the teacher's fee.
yaksha-prashna: At a lake, a yaksha put questions to the thirsty Pandavas; Yudhishthira's answers of dharma revived his four brothers.
karna-kavach-kundal: Knowing the brahmin was Indra in disguise, Karna cut off his god-given armour and earrings and gave them away.
abhimanyu-chakravyuh: Sixteen-year-old Abhimanyu broke into the Chakravyuha alone and fell fighting many great warriors at once.
vishnu-sahasranama-bhishma: Lying on the bed of arrows, Bhishma taught Yudhishthira the hymn of Vishnu's thousand names.
rigveda: The seer-families of the land of seven rivers composed 1,028 hymns to Agni, Indra and Soma: humanity's oldest living scripture.
yajnavalkya-maitreyi: As Yajnavalkya divided his wealth before renouncing, Maitreyi asked instead for the knowledge of immortality.
patanjali-yoga-sutra: In 195 aphorisms Maharshi Patanjali defined yoga as the stilling of the mind and gave the eightfold path.
shivratri-ekadashi-vrat: The Puranas and Dharmashastras set out the night vigil of Mahashivaratri for Shiva and the Ekadashi fast for Vishnu, open to all.
navratri-durga: Navaratri and the Autumn Durga Festival
Nine nights of Ashvin devoted to Mother Durga, the Devi Mahatmya recited, and the tenth day Vijayadashami celebrated as victory.
appar-tirunavukkarasar: Returning from the Jain order, Appar sang the hymns of the Tevaram and walked from temple to temple with a hoe to clear the grass.
sambandar: Fed by the Goddess at three and singing at once, Sambandar composed Tevaram hymns at over two hundred temples before he was sixteen.
manikkavasagar-thiruvasagam: The minister who spent the royal treasury on a Shiva temple, Manikkavacakar composed the Tiruvacakam, hymns said to melt a heart of stone.
nammalvar-thiruvaimozhi: Silent for sixteen years in the hollow of a tamarind tree, Nammalvar sang the 1,102 verses of the Tiruvaymoli, called the Tamil Veda.
madhavdev-namghosa: Srimanta Sankardev's chief disciple Madhavdev composed the Namghosha and the Borgeet, still sung in Assam's namghars.
krittivasi-ramayan: Krittivas Ojha recast the Ramayana in singable Bengali verse, the Rama-katha of every Bengali home.
akkalkot-swami-samarth: Revered as an avatar of Dattatreya, Swami Samarth lived at Akkalkot from 1856 to 1878; his words: fear not, I am behind you.
bamakhepa-tarapith: Bamakhepa, devoted to Mother Tara, practised in the cremation ground of Tarapith; people called him the Mother's mad son.
morya-gosavi: The chief Ganapatya saint walked every month from Chinchwad to Morgaon; Ganpati Bappa Morya carries his name.
janabai-muktabai: Namdev's servant Janabai, Dnyaneshwar's sister Muktabai and Chokhamela's wife Soyarabai: the first women saint-poets of Marathi.
akka-mahadevi: Taking Chennamallikarjuna (Shiva) alone as her husband, Akka Mahadevi left the palace and reached the Anubhava Mantapa at Kalyana.
raghavendra-swami-mantralayam: In 1671 the Dvaita saint Raghavendra Tirtha entered his brindavana alive at Mantralayam on the Tungabhadra.
sharada-peeth-kashmir: This seat of Goddess Sarasvati was among India's greatest centres of learning; the Sharada script and Kashmir's name Sharada-desha come from it.
pashupatinath: On the Bagmati, Pashupatinath is Nepal's guardian lord; Licchavi inscriptions call him master of the valley.
dwadash-jyotirlinga: The Shiva Purana lists twelve jyotirlingas, where Shiva appeared as an endless pillar of light, from Somnath to Rameswaram.
51-shaktipeeth: All of India and neighbouring lands
Wherever the parts of Sati's body fell, a Shakti Peetha arose: from Kashmir to Kanyakumari and from Hinglaj to Kamakhya.
char-dham-bharat: Badrinath in the north, Dwarka in the west, Puri in the east and Rameswaram in the south: the four abodes at India's four corners.
vishnupad-gaya: The great tirtha of ancestral rites, where Ahilyabai Holkar built a temple in 1787 over Vishnu's footprint in rock.
rath-yatra: Deities ride chariots through the town; at Puri the great chariots of Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra go each year to the Gundicha temple.
tripurasur-vadh: With a single arrow Mahadev burned the three flying cities of Tarakasura's sons and became Tripurari.
lingodbhava: Lingodbhava, the Endless Pillar of Light
Between Brahma and Vishnu appeared an endless pillar of fire whose ends neither could find: the origin of the Shiva-linga.
putana-makhan-chor: The infant Krishna ended the demoness Putana; growing up, he stole butter from every home in Gokul.
chitrakoot-kamadgiri: Shri Ram spent much of his exile at Chitrakoot on the Mandakini; the circuit of Kamadgiri hill is believed to fulfil wishes.
gokarna-mahabaleshwar: Ganesha, as a boy, set down the Atmalinga here to keep it from Ravana; Gokarna also appears in the Mahabharata's tirtha list.
gangasagar-kapil-muni: Where the Ganga meets the sea, King Sagara's sixty thousand sons were freed; at Makar Sankranti India's great bathing fair gathers here.
chhath-mahaparv: A four-day vow to the Sun: standing in water to offer arghya to the setting and rising sun, the great folk festival of Bihar and Purvanchal.
kanyakumari-devi: At India's southern tip the Goddess Kumari waits in penance to wed Shiva; the 1st-century Greek Periplus already mentions pilgrims bathing here.
palani-murugan: Angered at losing the fruit of wisdom, young Murugan left Kailash and stands on Palani hill as an ascetic with a staff.
tiruchendur-murugan: Murugan's only seaside abode, where he defeated the demon Surapadma; the Soorasamharam of Skanda Shashti is grandest here.
pongal-makar-sankranti: The festival of the sun turning north: Pongal in Tamil Nadu, Lohri in Punjab, Uttarayan in Gujarat, Magh Bihu in Assam, Khichdi in Bihar.
vindhyavasini-mirzapur: The girl-child who slipped from Kamsa's hands on Krishna's birth night, Yogamaya, dwells on the Vindhya hills as Vindhyavasini.
arunachaleswarar-tiruvannamalai: Arunachala hill, worshipped as the fire-linga, is held to be Shiva himself; at Karthigai Deepam a great flame is lit on its summit.
srikalahasti-kannappa: The wind-linga named for a spider, a snake and an elephant; here the hunter Kannappa offered his eyes to Shiva.
kanchi-kamakshi: Kamakshi, presiding goddess of Kanchi, sits in lotus pose; tradition says Adi Shankaracharya installed the Sri Chakra here.
kolhapur-mahalakshmi: Ambabai of Karvir: in this temple begun in the Chalukya age, twice a year the setting sun's rays fall straight on the goddess's feet.
naina-devi-himachal: A Shakti Peetha on a Shivalik peak where Sati's eyes are believed to have fallen, overlooking Gobind Sagar lake.
kollur-mookambika: Mookambika, slayer of Mookasura, is worshipped in a jyotirlinga as Shiva and Shakti together; tradition says Shankaracharya installed the Sri Chakra here.
sringeri-sharadamba: On the Tunga, the first matha founded by Adi Shankaracharya and the abode of Sharadamba, goddess of learning.
mehandipur-balaji: In an Aravalli valley, the shrine of Balaji (Hanuman), Pretraj Sarkar and Bhairav: a centre of faith for relief from spirit afflictions and distress.
ambaji-shaktipeeth: Mother Amba's shrine in the Arasur hills, where no idol stands in the sanctum, only the Shri Visa Yantra.
pavagadh-kalika: The ancient Shakti Peetha of Kalika Mata on Pavagadh hill; in 2022 a flag flew on its spire again after five centuries.
hinglaj-mata: A Shakti Peetha in a cave among Makran's desert hills; Hindus and local Muslims alike revere it as Nani Mandir.
simhachalam-narasimha: The hilltop Varaha-Lakshmi-Narasimha stays covered in sandal paste all year; his true form is seen only at Chandanotsavam on Akshaya Tritiya.
tulja-bhavani: Kuldevi of Chhatrapati Shivaji; tradition says the Goddess blessed him with the Bhavani sword.
maihar-sharda-mata: Mother Sharada atop 1,063 steps on Trikut hill; folk belief says Alha still comes first to worship at dawn.
jejuri-khandoba: Malhari Martand Khandoba, a folk form of Shiva, worshipped amid showers of yellow turmeric and the cry Yelkot Yelkot Jai Malhar.
pushkar-brahma: The best-known of Brahma's rare temples; Pushkar lake is held to have formed where a lotus fell from Brahma's hand.
ahobilam-nava-narasimha: Where Lord Narasimha is believed to have burst from the pillar and slain Hiranyakashipu; nine Narasimha shrines in the Nallamala hills.
ramdevra-baba-ramdev: The Tanwar saint Baba Ramdev took living samadhi here; Hindus honour him as an avatar of Krishna and Muslims as Ramsa Pir.
majuli-satra: On the Brahmaputra's largest river island, sattras founded in Sankardev's wake keep alive the namghar, Sattriya dance, Bhaona drama and mask-making.
sankat-mochan-varanasi: By the Assi river, where tradition says Goswami Tulsidas had darshan of Hanuman and founded this temple.
kumbakonam-mahamaham: Where the pot of nectar broke after the deluge lies the Mahamaham tank; every twelve years it hosts the Kumbh of the south.
mathura-krishna-janmabhoomi: Believed birthplace of Krishna in Kamsa's prison; in 1618 Bir Singh Bundela of Orchha built the great Keshavdev temple here.
barsana-radha-rani: Village of Radha's father Vrishabhanu; the Ladli ji temple crowns Bhanugarh hill, and its Lathmar Holi is world-famous.
shani-shingnapur: Shani Dev as a black stone under the open sky; belief holds that the village's houses need no doors or locks.
bihu-assam: Assam's three Bihus: Rongali in Baisakh (new year), Kongali in Kartik and Bhogali in Magh, festivals of farming, dance and dhol-pepa.
shri-govindajee-imphal: By a dream-command, Rajarshi Bhagyachandra had Govindaji carved from a jackfruit tree on Kaina hill; the heart of Manipur's Vaishnavism.
manipuri-ras-leela: In 1779 Rajarshi Bhagyachandra staged the first Ras Leela before Govindaji, his daughter Bimbavati as Radha; it is now one of India's classical dances.
hanumangarhi-ayodhya: Hanuman is believed to guard Ayodhya from here; pilgrims visit Hanumangarhi before Ram Lalla.
jwalamukhi-shaktipeeth: No idol here: the Goddess is worshipped in nine eternal flames rising from the rock; in 1815 Maharaja Ranjit Singh gilded the temple's dome.
tarapith-temple: Mother Tara's tantric seat on the Dwaraka river, where Vashishtha and Bamakhepa practised in the great cremation ground.
chamundeshwari-mysore: Chamundeshwari, slayer of Mahishasura, is kuldevi of Mysore's Wadiyar kings; Mysore (Mahishuru) is named after the demon.
yamunotri-dham: First stop of the Chhota Char Dham, source of the Yamuna; rice and potatoes are cooked as prasad in the boiling Surya Kund.
kheer-bhawani-tulmul: The Goddess Ragnya in a spring whose waters change colour; the greatest shrine of Kashmiri Pandits.
kanwar-yatra: In Sawan, devotees carry Ganga water on a kanwar on foot to their Shiva temple: a pilgrimage of crores from Haridwar to Deoghar.
parshuram-kund: A bath in this Lohit river pool is believed to have washed away Parashurama's sin; a great Makar Sankranti fair of the North-East.
nageshwar-jyotirlinga: Shiva appeared as Nageshwar in the demoness Daruka's forest to save his devotee Supriya: the jyotirlinga near Dwarka.
girnar-dattatreya: The sacred mountain of some 10,000 steps, with peaks of Ambaji, Gorakhnath and Dattatreya's footprints; a tirtha for Hindus and Jains.
prayagraj-mahakumbh: At the confluence of Ganga, Yamuna and Sarasvati, humanity's largest gathering; crores bathed over 45 days at the 2025 Maha Kumbh.
karaikkal-ammaiyar: One of the earliest Tamil poet-saints of Shiva; Shiva himself called her Amma, mother. About the 6th century.
mudhal-alvars: The First Three Alvars at Tirukkovalur
Poygai, Bhutam and Pey sheltered in a tiny porch on a stormy night and felt Vishnu himself press in as the fourth. About the 6th–7th century.
sundarar-tiruttondattogai: Third of the great Tevaram poets, called Shiva's friend by tradition; he sang the list of the 63 Nayanars. About 680 CE.
periyalvar-kulasekhara: Periyalvar sang lullabies to child Krishna as Yashoda and raised Andal; the Chera king Kulasekhara wrote the Mukundamala. About the 8th century.
tirumangai-alvar: The chieftain Kaliyan turned saint: he composed the most hymns of the Divya Prabandham and sang of more than 80 of the 108 Divya Desams. About the 8th century (estimated).
adi-shankaracharya-janm: Shankara was born to Shivaguru and Aryamba at Kaladi on the Purna (Periyar). Traditionally 788 CE; scholars also suggest about 700–750 CE.
shankara-sannyas-govindapada: Shankara Takes Sannyasa and Finds Govindapada
A crocodile let go only when his mother agreed to his renunciation; on the Narmada, in a cave at Omkareshwar, Shankara found his guru Govindapada. Traditional account.
manisha-panchakam: Shankara and the Chandala at Kashi
Asked to step aside on the way to the Ganga, the outcaste asked: who should move, the body or the self? Shankara answered with the Manisha Panchakam. Traditional account.
shankar-mandan-mishra-shastrarth: Shankara Debates Mandana Mishra, Ubhaya Bharati as Judge
Shankara debated the Mimamsa scholar Mandana Mishra with Mandana's wife Ubhaya Bharati as judge; defeated, Mandana became the monk Sureshvaracharya. Traditional account.
nathamuni-divya-prabandham: Nathamuni recovered the forgotten four thousand hymns of the Alvars, set them to music and had them sung in temples beside the Veda. About 900 CE.
yamunacharya-alavandar: Nathamuni's grandson won half a kingdom in debate as a boy, then gave it up to serve Ranganatha; Ramanuja became his successor. About the 10th century.
khajuraho-lakshmana-temple: Built by the Chandella king Yashovarman and consecrated under Dhanga in 954 CE, the earliest and best preserved of Khajuraho's great temples.
mukteshvara-temple-bhubaneswar: A small 10th-century Shiva temple whose carved arched gateway is unique in Odisha; called the gem of Kalinga architecture.
ramanujacharya-janm: Ramanuja was born at Sriperumbudur to Asuri Keshava Somayaji and Kantimati. Traditionally 1017–1137 CE (120 years); scholars place him about 1077–1157 CE.
gangaikonda-cholapuram: After his campaign to the Ganga, Rajendra Chola founded a new capital and built this great Shiva temple in the 1030s.
bhojeshwar-temple-bhojpur: An unfinished 11th-century Shiva temple linked to the Paramara king Bhoja, whose huge linga is among the largest in India.
ramanuja-tirukoshtiyur-mantra: Given the eight-syllable mantra on a promise of secrecy, Ramanuja climbed the temple tower and proclaimed it to everyone. Traditional account.
belur-chennakeshava: Begun in 1117 by the Hoysala king Vishnuvardhana, the temple of handsome Keshava is carved as finely as ivory.
halebidu-hoysaleswara: A twin-shrine Shiva temple begun about 1121 at the Hoysala capital Dorasamudra, its walls carved with the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Bhagavata.
basavanna-janm: Birth of Basavanna, founder of the Lingayat tradition, who taught Shiva-bhakti, the dignity of work and equality of caste and gender. About 1131 CE (some traditions give 1105).
darasuram-airavatesvara: Shiva temple built by Rajaraja Chola II (1146–1173), its hall shaped like a stone chariot with wheels and horses.
ramappa-temple: Built in 1213 by the Kakatiya general Recherla Rudra, the Ramalingeshwara temple is known by the name of its sculptor, Ramappa.
madhvacharya-janm: Vasudeva, later Madhvacharya, was born at Pajaka near Udupi. Traditionally 1238–1317 CE.
somanathapura-keshava: Built in 1258 by Somanatha, general of the Hoysala king Narasimha III: a three-shrine temple on a star-shaped platform.
dnyaneshwar-sanjeevan-samadhi: At twenty-one, Sant Dnyaneshwar entered living samadhi at Alandi on the Indrayani. Traditionally Kartik Krishna Trayodashi, 1296 CE.
guru-nanak-janm: Nanak was born at Talwandi to Mehta Kalu and Mata Tripta; he became the first Sikh Guru and taught devotion to Ik Onkar. 1469 CE.
meerabai-janm: Born into the Rathore family of Merta and married into the royal house of Mewar, Mira's heart belonged to Giridhar Gopal from childhood. About 1498 CE.
tripura-sundari-temple: In 1501 Maharaja Dhanya Manikya built the Tripura Sundari temple on a tortoise-backed hill; tradition counts it among the 51 Shakti Peethas.
chaitanya-mahaprabhu-sannyas: In 1510, at twenty-four, Nimai, the kirtan leader of Navadvip, took sannyasa from Keshava Bharati at Katwa and became Shri Krishna Chaitanya.
haridas-thakur: Haridasa Thakur, Teacher of the Holy Name
Chaitanya's close companion who chanted three lakh names daily; the biographies say he was born in a Muslim family. About 1510 CE.
lepakshi-temple: Built in the 1530s by Virupanna and Viranna, officers of the Vijayanagara king Achyuta Raya; famed for painted ceilings, a hanging pillar and a giant Nandi.
tulsidas-janm: The poet of the Ramcharitmanas is said to have been born on Shravan Shukla Saptami at Rajapur. Traditionally 1532 CE; other dates such as 1497 and 1511 are also given. Soron is also named as his birthplace.
mangueshi-temple: In 1560, during Portuguese persecution, devotees secretly carried the Mangesh linga from Kushasthali (Cortalim) to Priol; it is now Goa's most famous temple.
orchha-ram-raja: Queen Ganesh Kunwari brought Rama from Ayodhya; set down in the palace, the image would not move, and Rama became king of Orchha. Traditional account.
tukaram-beej: Varkari tradition holds that in 1650, on Phalgun Krishna Dwitiya, Tukaram left for Vaikuntha in his body; the day is kept as Tukaram Beej.
aihole-temples: About a hundred temples of the 6th–8th centuries under the early Chalukyas, where northern and southern styles were first tried out.
pattadakal-temples: The Chalukya coronation site where Nagara and Dravida temples stand side by side; Queen Lokamahadevi built the Virupaksha temple about 745 CE.
deogarh-dashavatara-temple: A Gupta-period Vishnu temple of about 500 CE, among the first stone temples with a tower over the sanctum: the start of the north Indian temple form.
mundeshwari-temple: An octagonal stone temple on a Kaimur hill, counted among the oldest temples in continuous worship in India; about the 6th–7th century (estimated).
katas-raj: Katas Raj, Pool of Shiva's Tears
Temples around a sacred pool in the Salt Range; tradition says the pool formed from Shiva's tears at Sati's death.
onam-mahabali: Kerala's harvest festival, when by tradition King Mahabali returns once a year to meet his people. Tiruvonam is mentioned in the Sangam-era Maduraikkanchi.
shankaracharya-temple-srinagar: The ancient Jyeshtheshwara Shiva temple on Gopadri hill above Dal Lake, now called the Shankaracharya temple; tradition says Adi Shankara came here.
jageshwar-dham: Over a hundred stone temples in a deodar forest; some traditions regard it as the Nagesh jyotirlinga. From about the 8th century (estimated).
unakoti: Unakoti, One Short of a Crore
Giant rock-cut images of Shiva and gods in the forest, with a Shiva head about 30 feet high at the centre. About the 7th–9th century (on style).
karthigai-deepam: The festival of lamps on the Krittika star in Kartik; a great lamp is lit atop Arunachala. Chola inscriptions record gifts for it, and early Tamil poetry mentions it.
ashtavinayak: Eight self-manifested Ganesha shrines around Pune (Morgaon, Siddhatek, Pali, Mahad, Theur, Lenyadri, Ozar and Ranjangaon), cared for by the Peshwas in the 18th century.
dakor-ranchhodrai: The Ranchhodrai temple at Dakor; tradition says the devotee Bodana brought the Lord here from Dwarka. The present temple was built in 1772 by the Maratha official Gopalrao Tambvekar.
swami-vivekananda-janm: Narendranath Datta was born in Kolkata on 12 January 1863 to Vishwanath Datta and Bhuvaneshwari Devi; the day is India's National Youth Day.
ramakrishna-vivekananda-bhent: Late in 1881 the eighteen-year-old Narendra asked Sri Ramakrishna at Dakshineswar: have you seen God? The answer: yes, more clearly than I see you.
ramana-maharshi-atma-bodh: In July 1896, sixteen-year-old Venkataraman was seized by a fear of death in Madurai and in that moment knew that the body dies, not the I. Six weeks later he left for Arunachala.
